title: AI Agent Cost Management: Budgets, Attribution, and Cost per Task
excerpt: Control AI agent spending with atomic reservations, complete cost attribution, uncertain-charge recovery, and metrics tied to successful task outcomes.
content:
AI agent cost management starts before a request is sent. An agent can expand a task into repeated model calls, paid searches, browser sessions, and subagents. A monthly billing chart reveals the result, but it cannot decide whether the next branch is affordable. That decision needs an application-level budget tied to the task and its expected outcome.

This guide proposes a reservation ledger for controlling spend and a separate accounting view for assessing value. Its workflow, thresholds, and dollar figures are hypothetical engineering examples, not current provider prices or measured production results.

## Distinguish four different kinds of limit

A token limit bounds a model request. A throughput quota controls admission over time. A money budget controls authorized expenditure. A business target defines an acceptable cost for an outcome. These constraints interact, but one does not substitute for another.

For example, Amazon Bedrock documents initial token-quota deductions based partly on the requested output limit, followed by adjustments as actual usage becomes known. Its quota calculations can differ from billable token accounting. Do not interpret an available quota balance as an available cash balance. [Amazon Bedrock token accounting](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html).

Likewise, Google Cloud distinguishes alerts-only budgets from supported spend-cap budgets. Alerts-only budgets do not automatically stop spending, and billing information and notifications can arrive after resource use. An application needing immediate per-task control should enforce its own admission policy rather than wait for a billing alert. [Google Cloud budgets and budget alerts](https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets).

Keep [rate limiting and backpressure](/blog/ai-agent-rate-limits-backpressure) coordinated with cost admission: a request must satisfy both capacity and expenditure constraints before dispatch.

## Model the entire task cost

Represent each billable operation separately. For a model call, an illustrative estimator is:

```text
estimated_call_cost =
  uncached_input_tokens × input_rate
  + cached_input_tokens × cached_input_rate
  + maximum_output_tokens × output_rate
  + applicable_request_fees
```

This is a conceptual formula. Real providers may distinguish cache creation, cache reads, reasoning, media, deployment modes, or other charge categories. Version the rate configuration with currency, effective date, provider, model, and billing mode. Preserve the version used for each estimate so a later price change does not rewrite historical assumptions.

Add search fees, embedding requests, database usage, sandbox compute, browser time, storage, and network transfer where relevant. A cheap model can initiate an expensive tool. A failed operation can still consume resources. A cancelled stream can already have generated billable work.

Maintain separate views for direct variable expense and allocated shared expense. A marginal routing decision might use direct cost; a product sustainability review may include platform operation and human review. State which view a dashboard displays.

## Reserve before starting concurrent work

A common race appears when several workers read the same remaining budget. Each sees enough money for its own request, then all dispatch. Checking a balance is insufficient unless the check and reservation happen atomically.

In this proposed ledger, each task has a budget, settled charges, outstanding reservations, and a revision. Admission succeeds only when:

```text
settled + outstanding_reservations + proposed_reservation <= authorized_budget
```

Implement the condition with a transaction or conditional update, not a read followed by an unrelated write. Give each reservation a stable operation identifier. Repeated delivery of the same dispatch event must retrieve the existing reservation rather than allocate it again.

Reserve a conservative request envelope using bounded input, an enforced output maximum, and known tool caps. A reservation based only on average usage is a soft estimate, not a hard expenditure guarantee. If a provider operation has no enforceable upper bound, either reserve a documented worst case, obtain a larger allowance, or label the control as approximate.

The reservation does not itself contact the provider. Persist its relationship to dispatch so a crash cannot make an initiated request disappear from accounting. A dispatcher may safely retry delivery only under a defined operation contract.

## Worked example: a research task with a five-cent budget

Assume a fictional service authorizes $0.050 for one task. Its fictional model rates are $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens. These are deliberately illustrative rates.

The proposed plan reserves:

| Stage | Reserved amount | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coordinator | $0.009 | 1,500 input and at most 1,000 output tokens |
| Two research workers | $0.022 | Each: 2,500 input and at most 1,000 output tokens |
| Paid retrieval | $0.004 | Explicit tool request allowance |
| Final synthesis | $0.010 | Bounded envelope under the fictional rates |
| Remaining headroom | $0.005 | Uncommitted allowance |

The plan fits because committed envelopes total $0.045. A third worker would require another $0.011, bringing the planned total to $0.056. The admission service rejects that branch before it starts. The coordinator may reduce scope or ask for a larger authorized budget; it cannot silently borrow from final synthesis.

Suppose actual coordinator, worker, retrieval, and synthesis charges settle at $0.006, $0.017, $0.004, and $0.008. The total is $0.035. Settlement releases the difference between each reservation and its confirmed charge, leaving $0.015 unused.

This arithmetic demonstrates a policy, not a forecast. Quality still needs evaluation: two workers may be insufficient for the question. Anthropic reports increased token usage for its own multi-agent research system and emphasizes that task value must justify that expenditure. Its reported behavior is evidence about that system, not a universal multiplier for your budget. [Anthropic’s multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/research/multi-agent-research-system).

## Settle uncertainty without inventing a refund

After a successful response, record provider-reported usage and calculate the corresponding charge under the applicable rate configuration. Keep the estimate and settlement as distinct events. If a later invoice differs, append a reconciliation adjustment instead of overwriting history.

A timeout creates an uncertain liability. The provider may have accepted the request and completed work after the client disconnected. Mark the reservation unresolved; do not immediately release it and allow another call to spend the same allowance. Query available usage records, reconcile with provider identifiers, and apply a documented expiry or conservative charge policy when final evidence remains unavailable.

Cancellation has the same accounting problem. Stopping a worker prevents future dispatch; it does not reverse charges already incurred. Show outstanding liabilities beside settled spend so operators can distinguish a quiet system from a fully reconciled one.

Use [agent observability traces](/blog/ai-agent-observability-tracing) to connect execution to ledger events, while treating the durable ledger as the accounting record. Sampled traces alone cannot reliably account for every charge.

## Attribute costs at the operation boundary

Attach server-controlled task, tenant, workflow-version, stage, operation, and provider-request identifiers when work starts. Do not let a model choose the tenant to bill. Record retries as separate attempts beneath the same logical operation; hiding them makes an unreliable workflow appear inexpensive.

A practical event record contains:

- Usage quantities with units, including separate cached and uncached categories when supplied.
- The rate version, currency, estimated amount, settled amount, and reconciliation status.
- Parent task and stage identifiers for fan-out attribution.
- Outcome class: useful result, rejected output, timeout, cancellation, or unresolved liability.

Avoid recording sensitive prompts merely to calculate cost. Aggregate operational metrics by bounded dimensions such as workflow and model; keep per-task identifiers in a controlled ledger or trace store rather than creating an unbounded metric series for every request.

## Optimize cost per successful outcome

The FinOps Foundation distinguishes resource-efficiency units from business units and recommends connecting technology costs to delivered value. For an agent, cost per token explains a resource rate; cost per correctly resolved task explains whether the workflow is economically useful. [FinOps Foundation: Unit Economics](https://www.finops.org/framework/capabilities/unit-economics/).

Define success before comparing routes. In a hypothetical evaluation of 1,000 equivalent tasks, Route A costs $0.015 per attempt and succeeds on 600 tasks: $15 / 600 = $0.025 per success. Route B costs $0.022 per attempt and succeeds on 900: $22 / 900, approximately $0.0244 per success. The higher attempt cost yields a slightly lower successful-outcome cost in this invented example.

Include failed attempts in the numerator. Report escalation and human-review expenses separately or include them under an explicitly defined fully loaded metric. Segment by task difficulty and customer cohort; changes in traffic mix can otherwise masquerade as efficiency improvements. Also inspect tail costs, not just the mean: a small number of looping tasks can dominate expense.

## Validate the budget mechanism

Test the ledger with adversarial sequences before trusting a cap:

- Two workers concurrently reserve the final available allowance.
- A dispatch event is delivered twice.
- The process crashes after provider acceptance but before recording a response.
- Usage arrives late, without final token counts, or under a changed rate version.
- A cancelled worker returns a charge after the parent task closes.
- A retry chain reaches its allowance while synthesis capacity remains reserved.

Verify conservation of reservations and settlements after every sequence. Then compare application totals with provider usage and invoices over consistent time windows. Explain differences such as delayed reporting, discounts, taxes, currency conversion, and shared charges rather than forcing totals to match silently.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a maximum token count enough to cap agent cost?

It bounds part of one call. A task also needs limits on repeated calls, subagents, paid tools, and execution duration. Monetary enforcement depends on a valid rate model and enforceable operation envelopes.

### Should unused reservations expire automatically?

Only with a policy for uncertain work. Expiring a reservation while its request may still be running can authorize double spending. Separate a worker lease from the financial liability it created.

### Should every task receive the same budget?

No. Use authorized task classes and evaluated service levels. A simple lookup and an open-ended investigation have different value and uncertainty. Keep the allocation policy outside model control and expose scope reductions when a budget is insufficient.
